summary: Describes the RTP/AVP profile for using RTP version 2 and RTCP in audio and video conferences with minimal control. It explains how generic RTP fields apply to audio and video and defines default payload types. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RTP carries audio and video over the Internet, but the base specification leaves many choices open. This RFC fixes those choices for conferences that need no negotiation: it says which sound or picture format each payload type number means, and how the RTP and RTCP packets should behave. Conference tools that follow the same profile can then talk to each other without extra setup.

which rtp payload types are dynamic
subtitle: The default rulebook for carrying audio and video over RTP when nothing is negotiated, including the numbered list of codecs.

tldr.problem: RTP leaves many details open, such as what each payload type number means and how the control traffic should behave, so two conference tools could not interoperate without extra agreement.
tldr.mechanism: This profile, named RTP/AVP, fills in those blanks for audio and video conferences with minimal control: it fixes defaults for the RTP and RTCP header fields and binds static payload type numbers to a set of named encodings.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 1890 and has been updated by RFC 5761, RFC 7007 and RFC 8860. It also closes the list of static payload types, so new encodings use dynamic payload types instead.

today: RFC 3551 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 5761, RFC 7007 and RFC 8860. It obsoleted RFC 1890.

sections.title: What the Profile Is For
sections.content:
The Real-time Transport Protocol, defined in RFC 3550, deliberately leaves some choices to a profile. This document is the profile called RTP/AVP. It is meant for audio and video conferences with minimal session control: it provides no negotiation of parameters and no membership control.

The profile works in sessions that use static payload types and the membership information that RTCP already gives. It can also be combined with a higher-level control protocol. Other profiles may make different choices for the same items.

The RFC also describes a set of audio and video encodings and the way each is packed into RTP, simply because each description is too small to deserve its own document. Using those payload formats is NOT REQUIRED. Only the binding of some of them to static payload type numbers in Tables 4 and 5 is normative.
sections.plainLanguage: RTP leaves some choices open. This RFC is one fixed set of answers, for audio and video calls that need no negotiation. It says which payload type numbers stand for which encodings, and how the RTP and RTCP packets should look.

sections.title: RTP and RTCP Behavior Under the Profile
sections.content:
Section 2 walks through the list of items that RTP says a profile may set. Generally the profile follows the defaults. The standard fixed RTP header is used with one marker bit, no extra fixed fields are added, and no new RTCP packet types are defined. Header extensions are not defined, but applications MAY use them, so they SHOULD NOT assume the X bit is always zero.

The RTCP traffic bandwidth MAY be set as its own session parameter. Following the RTP recommendation that one quarter of RTCP bandwidth go to data senders, the RECOMMENDED defaults are 1.25% for senders and 3.75% for the rest. For participants that do not send data, it MAY be set to zero on unidirectional links, but the sender share SHOULD stay non-zero so sender reports can still support synchronization and identify the source by CNAME.

Applications MAY use any SDES item. CNAME MUST be sent every reporting interval, while the other items SHOULD be sent only every third interval, with NAME sent seven times out of eight in that slot.

On congestion, receivers SHOULD watch packet loss. Under best-effort service, loss is acceptable if a TCP flow on the same path would get no less throughput than the RTP flow. The comparison is meant as an order-of-magnitude one, and an application that consumes bandwidth arbitrarily and does not compete fairly with TCP is not acceptable on the best-effort Internet. The profile uses RTP over unicast and multicast UDP as well as TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile keeps the normal RTP and RTCP packets and sets a few defaults, including how much of the session bandwidth is reserved for the control reports. It also tells receivers to watch for packet loss and to slow down when the network is congested, so the call competes fairly with ordinary data traffic.

sections.title: Static and Dynamic Payload Types
sections.content:
Every RTP data packet carries a payload type (PT) number that says which encoding the data uses. This profile assigns static numbers to some encodings and gives each encoding a short name that protocols such as SDP can use. Names can also be registered as MIME subtypes, and RFC 3555 registers all the names listed here.

The static number space is small, so payload types 96 to 127 are reserved for dynamic assignment through a conference control protocol or SDP, and applications SHOULD use them first. A dynamic binding applies only to the RTP session in which it is made, so the numbers can be reused in other sessions. Dynamic types SHOULD NOT be used without a well-defined way to indicate the mapping.

This RFC sets the policy that no more static payload types will be assigned beyond those in Tables 4 and 5. Some numbers are marked reserved: 1 and 2, 19, and the range 72 to 76, which is kept clear so RTCP and RTP packets can be told apart. Payload type 13 is the comfort noise payload format of RFC 3389.

Each payload type belongs to one media type: audio (A), video (V) or audio and video combined (AV). Payload types of different media types SHALL NOT be interleaved or multiplexed in one RTP session, though several RTP sessions MAY run in parallel. Audio applications SHOULD at least be able to send or receive payload types 0 (PCMU) and 5 (DVI4), which allows interoperability without format negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet carries a small number that names the encoding inside. A short list of numbers is fixed for good, and a small range at the top is chosen fresh for each session, so new formats never run out of numbers. A few reserved numbers keep RTP packets distinguishable from RTCP packets.

sections.title: Rules for Sending Audio
sections.content:
Silence suppression MAY be used with any audio payload format, and receivers MUST assume senders may do it. Because the RTP header has both a sequence number and a timestamp, a receiver can tell a lost packet from a quiet period. The first packet of a talkspurt SHOULD have its marker bit set to one, and senders that do not suppress silence MUST set it to zero. Where a format has no comfort noise frame of its own, the generic Comfort Noise payload format of RFC 3389 can be used.

The RTP clock rate is independent of the channel count. Channels are numbered left to right starting at one, and all samples from one sampling instant MUST be in the same packet. The sampling frequency SHOULD come from 8,000, 11,025, 16,000, 22,050, 24,000, 32,000, 44,100 and 48,000 Hz.

The default packetization interval SHOULD be 20 ms or one frame, whichever is longer. Longer packets cost less header overhead but add delay and make loss more noticeable. A receiver SHOULD accept packets holding between 0 and 200 ms of audio.

For sample-based encodings, multi-octet samples SHOULD be sent in network byte order, and the timestamp reflects the instant of the first sample. For frame-based encodings, packets SHALL contain a whole number of frames, oldest first, and the timestamp reflects the first sample of the first frame.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender may stop sending packets while nobody is speaking. A flag on the first packet after a pause tells the receiver that speech has started again. The profile also fixes how much audio goes in one packet, normally 20 milliseconds, which sets the minimum delay.

sections.title: The Audio and Video Encodings
sections.content:
Section 4.5 describes how each audio encoding is carried. Examples are PCMU and PCMA (G.711, 8 bits per sample, mu-law and A-law), DVI4, G722, G723, G726, G728, G729, GSM, L8 and L16, LPC, MPA, QCELP, RED and VDVI. For a few codecs it gives exact bit packing. Notable details are that G722 uses an RTP clock rate of 8,000 Hz even though its sampling rate is 16,000 Hz, because that value was assigned in RFC 1890 and must stay for backward compatibility, and that PCMA and PCMU MUST always be sent as 8-bit samples.

Video encodings are CelB, JPEG, H261, H263, H263-1998, MPV, MP2T and nv. They mostly point to the RFC that defines the payload format. All use an RTP timestamp frequency of 90,000 Hz, which gives exact timestamp steps for common frame rates, and 90 kHz is RECOMMENDED for future video encodings. The marker bit SHOULD be set to one in the last packet of a video frame, and all packets of one image share a timestamp. New H.263 implementations are advised to prefer the H263-1998 payload format.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists the sound and picture formats it covers and says how each compressed piece is placed in a packet. Video uses a clock that ticks 90,000 times a second, which divides evenly into the usual television frame rates. One sound codec keeps a historical 8,000 Hz RTP clock even though it samples at 16,000 Hz.

sections.title: Ports and Byte Streams
sections.content:
RTP data SHOULD go on an even UDP port and the matching RTCP packets on the next higher, odd port. Applications MAY use any such pair, for example one allocated at random by a session manager, because a single fixed pair cannot be required when several applications share a host.

Ports 5004 and 5005 are registered for this profile as an optional default pair. Applications need not have a default.

If RTP must run over TCP or another byte stream, the application MUST define its own way of delimiting RTP and RTCP packets. The RFC points to RTSP as an example of such an encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: RTP data uses one even-numbered UDP port, and the control reports use the next, odd port. Ports 5004 and 5005 are registered as an optional default pair for this profile.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1890
sections.content:
This RFC revises RFC 1890 and is mostly backward compatible, except for functions removed because two interoperable implementations were not found. Those were the 1016 audio payload format (static type 1, now reserved) and the mapping of a pass-phrase to an encryption key.

Added were static payload types 4, 12, 16, 17, 18 and 34, plus type 13 for comfort noise. The G721 format was renamed G726-32, and type 2 is now deprecated and reserved. G729D, G729E, GSM-EFR, RED and H263-1998 were added with dynamic types only. Congestion control requirements were added, the RTCP bandwidth may now be set separately, and the ambiguous four-channel quadrophonic ordering was dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: Compared with the previous edition, this RFC adds several new payload types, retires two rules that never got two working implementations, and adds the congestion control requirement.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The profile adds no security services of its own, so the considerations of RTP apply. Because compression is applied end to end, encryption can be done after compression with no conflict between the two.

One threat noted is denial of service against encodings whose decoding cost varies a lot: an attacker can inject pathological datagrams that are complex to decode and overload the receiver. A receiver can also be overloaded by too many packets in general. Network-layer authentication MAY be used to discard unwanted sources, although its own processing cost may be too high, and in multicast the source pruning of IGMPv3 and multicast routing protocols lets a receiver choose which sources reach it.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile adds no security of its own. One risk is a packet that is deliberately hard to decode, which can keep the receiver busy; discarding packets from unwanted senders helps against this.
